newsitem.title: UK: New British MPs bring hopes -- and headaches.
newsitem.headline: New British MPs bring hopes -- and headaches.

text.p: The first problem for the 419 Labour members swept into parliament this week by Tony Blair's landslide victory is where to sit.
Tradition has the ruling party sitting on one side of the House of Commons facing the opposition and other minor parties.
But even if they sit in the aisles and pack the green leather benches, there is just not room for them all.
The second problem is what to do.
Commentators are already predicting that after a highly disciplined campaign, the first thing on the mind of some Labour members may be rebellion.

One left-winger, Ken Livingstone, immediately broke the silence on economic issues he maintained during the campaign and said the obvious way to balance Britain's books would be a "substantial tax increase".

But the size of Blair's majority -- 179 seats -- and the departure of many older MPs at odds with his modernising vision is likely to give Blair a far smoother ride than he could have hoped for during the campaign.

Out into retirement have gone anti-European Labour MPs like former minister Peter Shore and in have come a wave of young Labour hopefuls, all fiercely loyal to Blair's dive to ditch old-style socialist dogma and build a centre-left movement.
The average age of Labour's new intake is 48. The youngest, at 24, is Claire Ward who also symbolises the biggest change in the new parliament -- a big increase in the number of women.
There will be 118 women out of the total 659 MPs, compared to just 62 in the last parliamen, and 101 of them are Labour.

The results is bound to be a change in the old, clubby atmosphere of parliament -- a change that Blair has long argued for -- as well as pressure for a change to late working hours which put a huge pressure on family life. Plans for a children's nursery are already being discussed.
With so many young MPs, anxious not to offend the leadership in the hope of ascending to ministerial rank one day, the new prime minister can count on their loyalty.

If there is rebellion, it is more likely to come from the "awkward squad" of old-style MPs who have not retired -- like Dennis Skinner, a socialist firebrand who is one of the most caustic, and enjoyable, parliamentary debaters.

Tough new disciplinary rules to prevent Labour MPs stepping out of line were rushed through before the election, giving Blair -- who has already shown a steely determination to deal with any one stepping out of line -- additional strength.
For the ousted Conservatives, the picture is not so clear.
There may be plenty of room on the opposition benches -- in fact their 165 MPs will not quite fill the first section of seats facing the government -- but the party is far from united.
Pro- and anti-Europeans are already circling for the party leadership being vacated by John Major and the split is mirrored in the ranks.
But pro-Europeans like former finance minister Kenneth Clarke are bitterly angry with the so-called Eurosceptics for their open disregard for party unity.
The Conservatives look like continuing their bitter feuds, while Blair's "new" Labour party will brook no dissent. As a Blair speechwriter might put it, "New Labour, same old story".
